extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent practitioners, judges, and law students (United States)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards for whether an alleged invention is new, useful, and of sufficient invention to support a patent under U.S. law (treatment of novelty, utility, combination claims, improvements, prior use, and burden of proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement (useful/not mischievous)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a patent must be 'useful' — capable of use and not injurious or mischievous to the well-being, good policy or sound morals of society; it must be capable of use for some beneficial purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'useful' is not a test of general utility as a sufficiency-of-invention standard; it distinguishes useful inventions from frivolous or mischievous ones. The fact that an invention is capable of use for some beneficial purpose is what matters; the degree (greater or smaller utility) is not determinative of patentability. (See discussion distinguishing purely commercial packaging/labeling that leaves the article unchanged as frivolous.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty requirement ('new' / not known or used by others)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter of a patent must be 'new' — a new art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or a new improvement upon one of these, 'discovered or invented' by the patentee and 'not known or used by others' before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject-matter must be substantially different from anything known or used before; where analogous or similar things existed previously, that substantial difference measures sufficiency. The statute's phrase 'not known or used by others before' is construed in the U.S. to mean not known or used by the public (others) before the patentee's discovery. Patent recitals (the applicant's oath) provide prima facie evidence of novelty under the 1836 Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of invention measured by result (not apparent skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining sufficiency of invention the character of the result, not the apparent amount of skill, ingenuity or thought, is examined; if the result is substantially different from what had been effected before, the invention is entitled to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts focus on whether the result achieved is materially new; apparent simplicity or low skill is not a bar and may even indicate excellence. Evidence that a defendant's device is better is only relevant to show substantive difference between inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of form/proportion not a discovery unless new effect produced
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply changing the form or the proportions of a machine or composition is not a discovery; a mere change of form/proportion will not be a patentable invention unless that change produces a different effect (a change of principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The qualifier 'simply' is important: if the altered form yields a new effect or principle, it is not 'simply' a change and may be patentable. (Marshal’s and other authorities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent cannot claim an effect only; must claim manner/modus operandi
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be for an effect alone (e.g., the admeasurement of time or the expansive operations of steam); it must be for a new mode, new application, or the peculiar operation/manner of producing that effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents cover a means or mode of producing an effect; if the effect was produced before by the same mode, the patent is invalid. The inventor’s exclusive right is for the particular modus operandi or device, not for the abstract end or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of known ingredients may be patentable if combination is new
rubrics_metrics.description: Where ingredients or materials have been used before, the true question is whether they have been used before in the same combination; a new combination that produces a new friction match (or other article) can be patentable even if individual ingredients were known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The simplicity of a combination is not an objection; producing a new result by simple means can constitute the highest class of invention. Whether the combination existed before is a factual question for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of claim: whole machine vs. improvement (patent limited to actual improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specific machine already exists and the patentee merely added an improvement, the patentee cannot claim the whole machine; the patent extends only to the actual improvement, not to the pre-existing machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adding the patented lever to a watch does not permit patenting the whole watch; improvements to steam engines likewise limited. The patenter’s right cannot exceed what he actually invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination-claims and aggregation of previously separate operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent claims a whole machine that combines several distinct operations or stages, it is not sufficient that the specific assembled machine did not exist before; if the different effects were previously produced in separate machines or by substantially the same application of machinery, combining them will not sustain a patent for the whole machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries must decide whether the principles (modes of operation) are new or whether the machine is only an aggregation of known elements producing no substantially different result. Whittemore/wood-carding example: identify distinct stages and compare to prior separate machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of an old machine to a new use is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying an old or well-known apparatus or machinery to a new purpose, without substantial novelty in the device itself, does not create a patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: a coffee-mill used to grind oats, a cotton gin to clean hemp, a loom used with a different yarn — if unaltered, such use alone does not make the machine patentable. The purpose is not patentable; the machinery must be new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and effect of prior knowledge/use (U.S. rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. law (as construed from the act of 1793 and adopted in the act of 1836), knowledge or use by others invalidates a patent only if that knowledge/use existed before the discovery by the patentee (i.e., not known or used by others before the discovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with the English rule where any prior knowledge/use before application suffices. The focus in U.S. decisions is on preventing inventors from withholding knowledge unduly and promoting early public use; prior public use before the inventor’s discovery vitiates the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use by another person defeats novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior use by one person other than the patentee is sufficient to show that the patentee was not the first inventor and will vitiate novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute’s use of 'others' means use by any person or persons other than the applicant; single-party prior use is sufficient to destroy novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and evidentiary status of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: When novelty is disputed, the patentee must offer some evidence of novelty (show in what his invention consists and that he produced the effect in the manner specified). The patent and the applicant’s oath are prima facie evidence of novelty, shifting the onus to the defendant to show lack of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slight evidence from the patentee suffices to create the prima facie case; then the party alleging want of novelty must prove defect. The act of 1836 requires an oath that the applicant believes himself the original and first inventor; courts have treated this as admissible evidence.
